Chapter 9: The Influence of Identity—How Who We Are Shapes What We Do
Underneath every choice we make, there's this quiet, almost whispering question: "What kind of person am I?"
Identity—how we see ourselves, and how we want others to see us—shapes our actions in ways that are sometimes obvious, but often sneakier than we realize.
Imagine someone who’s just joined a running club. At first, she’s not sure if she even fits in. But as she starts to think of herself as “a runner,” things begin to shift. Suddenly, she’s buying new shoes, setting her alarm early for group runs, maybe even changing what she eats.
Her new identity isn’t just a label—it becomes a guide, quietly steering her decisions, both big and small.
And identity isn’t only about the labels we pick for ourselves. It’s about the groups we join. Picture a teacher who feels truly proud of her profession. You’ll hear her defending education in casual conversations, maybe even when she didn’t plan to. Or think of a parent who wants to be seen as deeply involved—they end up volunteering at every school event.
That desire to live up to an identity—whether we chose it or it landed on us—can be a powerful motivator.
Sometimes, the way identity shapes our behavior can catch us off guard. There’s this story about a team of coworkers. When asked to describe themselves, some say, “I’m a creative.” Others go with, “I’m a problem-solver.”
Later, when a challenge pops up, each person tackles it in a way that fits their self-image. The creative one pitches a bold new idea. The problem-solver? They’re hunting for practical solutions.
It’s like their identities are quietly guiding their responses—without them even noticing.
But identity can trip us up, too. Let’s say someone believes, “I’m just not a math person.” She might duck out of opportunities to learn, even though she’s totally capable. Or maybe a guy prides himself on being fiercely independent—so he refuses help, even if he really needs it.
The stories we tell ourselves about who we are—they can open doors, or slam them shut.
And don’t forget social influence. We look to others to confirm our identities. A new hire, wanting to fit in, picks up on the team’s values and makes them her own. A teenager, searching for belonging, tries on different identities until one finally feels right.
Most of us don’t realize just how much our identity shapes our choices. We think we’re acting on what we like, or what we believe is right. But often, we’re simply trying to live up to a certain image of ourselves.
Here’s the key takeaway: when you start noticing how identity works, you get to choose identities that actually help you grow—and make you happier.
